analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to set a drinking water standard for perchlorate that protects pregnant women and children.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a Senate committee in 2008 but never got a vote on the Senate floor before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Perchlorate, the main ingredient in solid rocket fuel, contaminated water supplies in dozens of states. The bill would have forced the EPA, within months, to issue a health advisory and a legally enforceable national drinking water limit for perchlorate — a limit designed to protect pregnant women, infants, and children, whose thyroid function the chemical can disrupt. The bill's only requirement fell on the EPA and, indirectly, on water systems and polluters who would have to meet the new standard.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink contaminated water — especially pregnant women, infants, and children. The bill's findings note contamination at nearly 400 sites across the country, including 153 public water systems in 26 states, and cite CDC research showing that even low-level exposure can alter thyroid hormones in women with low iodine, a condition affecting roughly 36% of American women [S4]. A binding national standard would have required polluters and water systems to clean up or treat that water.

how_it_helps.text: Required EPA to publish, within 90 days, a perchlorate health advisory that is fully protective — with an adequate margin of safety — of pregnant women, infants, and children, accounting for body weight, exposure patterns, and all routes of exposure [S3][S4].

Required EPA to propose a national primary drinking water regulation within 9 months and finalize it within 18 months, replacing the non-binding 'Drinking Water Equivalent Level' of 24.5 parts per billion that the bill's findings said ignored vulnerable populations and newer CDC research [S3][S4].

The reported amendment softened the original deadlines — the 2007 version set a final rule for December 31, 2007; the reported version allowed 18 months — but kept the enforceable deadline structure [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Makers and users of perchlorate — chiefly defense and aerospace contractors responsible for rocket fuel waste — who would bear cleanup and liability costs, and public water systems with perchlorate contamination, which would have to install treatment or find new sources to meet a federal limit [S4]. The costs of compliance could ultimately reach water ratepayers in affected communities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rocket fuel polluters and water utilities

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls heavily on public water systems, and the cost of treating perchlorate-tainted water would likely be passed on to ratepayers in affected communities, including those far from the original polluters [S4].

The bill dictated hard statutory deadlines for EPA rulemaking, bypassing the agency's normal process for weighing new health data and treatment feasibility; critics on the committee filed minority views against the report [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes are real: the bill documented contamination in 153 public water systems and in food and breast milk, with thyroid effects on fetuses and infants. The main cost — treatment and cleanup — is the standard price of a enforceable drinking water limit, though the bill's rigid deadlines and its assignment of costs to water systems rather than solely to polluters are legitimate design criticisms.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved the bill with an amendment in September 2008 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but no senator ever brought it to the floor for a vote, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, joined by four Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee [S1][S6].
On July 31, 2008, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S6].
On September 24, 2008, the committee reported the bill with Senate Report 110-484, and minority views were filed — a sign committee Republicans opposed the reported version [S6].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 1055), the waiting line for floor consideration, but the Senate never debated or voted on it [S6].
The bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, with no action in the House ever taken [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and users of perchlorate, and their federal customers in the Defense Department, avoided a legally enforceable cleanup and treatment mandate for another Congress; EPA faced no deadline to set a drinking water limit, and affected water systems faced no new treatment costs.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and four cosponsors were all Democrats, and the committee's minority — Republicans — filed minority views against the report; no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.industry: Aerospace, defense, and chemical makers that produce or use perchlorate
industries.note: A binding drinking water standard would have created enforceable cleanup and treatment obligations for perchlorate contamination, whose principal source is solid rocket fuel waste. Their interest in keeping no standard ran against the health of people drinking the water.

Utilities with perchlorate in their systems would have faced the cost of treatment or new water sources to meet a federal limit, costs likely passed to ratepayers. Some utilities in contaminated communities would gain cleaner water and clear federal guidance.
Perchlorate users beyond rocket fuel; a federal limit would apply to contamination from their products as well, though the record does not show them opposing the bill.
